topic: RFC 8693 OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange for scope delegation
query: RFC 8693 OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange scope delegation 2026
title: RFC 8693 OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange Abstract
snippet: RFC 8693, published in January 2020, defines the OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange protocol, providing a standardized HTTP- and JSON-based mechanism for clients to request and obtain security tokens from authorization servers acting as Security Token Services (STS).
claim: RFC 8693 defines standardized OAuth 2.0 token exchange for scope-limited credential delegation.

topic: RFC 8693 scope reduction and privilege delegation mechanisms
query: RFC 8693 OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange scope delegation 2026
title: OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693) for Agent Delegation: A Worked Example | MojoAuth Blog
snippet: The Token Exchange grant implements RFC 8693, OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange and can be used to exchange tokens to a different scope, audience or subject. Regarding scope management specifically, Scope is an optional parameter that allows changing the scope of the supplied token, for the requested token. Scope can be used to decrease privileges carried by the input tokens.
claim: RFC 8693 token exchange allows scope reduction through Scope parameter to decrease carried privileges.

topic: MCP Authorization with RFC 8707 audience-bound tokens
query: MCP Authorization token exchange audience-bound credentials
title: MCP Authentication and Authorization Patterns
snippet: The control objective is that the client should ask for a token explicitly intended for one MCP server, and the resource server should reject any token whose audience does not match its own identifier. MCP clients must send the RFC 8707 resource parameter on every authorization and token request, identifying the MCP server the token is for.
claim: MCP Authorization uses RFC 8707 audience binding to restrict tokens to specific MCP servers.

topic: Token audience validation and replay prevention
query: MCP Authorization token exchange audience-bound credentials
title: MCP authentication and authorization implementation guide
snippet: The server must then validate that a token was issued specifically for it through audience validation, which stops a stolen or misdirected token from being replayed against a different service.
claim: Audience validation prevents token replay attacks by restricting each token to its intended service.

title: Verifiable Credentials: A Simple Guide to How They Work
snippet: The W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model defines a standard format for expressing credentials that is cryptographically secure, privacy-preserving, and decentralised, where verification doesn't depend on contacting the issuer.
claim: W3C Verifiable Credentials enable offline verification without contacting the issuer.

topic: Scoped token broker for sandbox isolation and principle of least privilege
query: short-lived scoped token broker agent sandbox isolation
title: Secure AI agents with scoped tokens, DPoP, tool-level policies, and human approvals.
snippet: Short-lived agent sessions are derived from the user session at task start with minutes in TTL and are non-refreshable by design, expiring when the task completes or when the wall-clock TTL expires. Additionally, each agent identity should be scoped to a single tenant or organization, with Org IDs encoded into every token, every log line, and every policy evaluation.
claim: Short-lived scoped tokens with minutes TTL enforce principle of least privilege per agent task and tenant.

topic: Credential brokering via proxy outside sandbox
query: short-lived scoped token broker agent sandbox isolation
title: Short-Lived Credentials and Brokered Tokens for AI Agents — Frank Winkler
snippet: Credential brokering uses proxies that sit outside the agent's sandbox — one for LLM calls, one for everything else — where the agent makes ordinary HTTP calls and each proxy attaches the real token at the network layer, ensuring the agent never holds the credential.
claim: Proxies outside sandbox attach credentials at network layer, preventing agent access to credentials.

topic: Agent authorization with delegation intent tracking

title: Understanding OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693) and Delegation Grants | martinuke0's Blog
snippet: An active Internet-Draft notes that "RFC 8693 does not define a token-local mechanism for proving that downstream delegation intent remains consistent with the original authorization scope", indicating ongoing discussions about enhancing scope delegation mechanisms beyond what RFC 8693 currently specifies.
claim: RFC 8693 lacks token-local delegation intent validation, indicating ongoing standardization efforts for scope consistency.
